To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the specific binding of [11C]-Ro 15-1789 to the central benzodiazepines receptor sites in human brain can be quantified using PET and the radioligand [11C] flumazenil.
the Bmax and K(d) values for benzodiazepines in the human brain were 62-73 nM and 3.6 to 6 nM respectively.
the binding sites for benzodiazepines are present in the brain and that the binding of the benzodiazepinediazepam is saturable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a quantitative analysis of the central benzodiazepines in the human brain in vivo, using PET and [11C] flumazenil.
the development of a method to quantify benzodiazepines in human brain, using PET.
the development and application of a method to measure the binding characteristics of benzodiazepam in human brain using PET and [11C]Ro 15-1787.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the specific binding sites of the central type benzodiazepines in the brain of a normal human subject were characterized using PET and the radioligand [11C]Ro 15-178.
[11C] flumazenil binds to central benzodiazepines with a Kd of 3.6 to 6.0 nM in human brain.

the Bmax and K values in cerebral cortex are about 62-74 nM and 4-5 nM, respectively, in the estimation of plasma free ligand and 13-15 nM, respectively in the estimation of the regional exchangeable pools.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the binding sites for benzodiazepines in the human brain are similar to those in other species, and that PET is a useful technique for quantitative analysis of the benzodiazepinic binding sites in the brain in vivo.
the Bmax and K(d) values of [11C]-Ro 15-178 in the human cortex and cerebellar cortex are 73 and 12 nM, respectively, in vivo and that the Bmax value of the cerebellum is 62 nM.
the Bmax value in cerebral cortex and cerebelum is about 62-75 nmol/l and Kd value is 3.6 nM, which is consistent with the results obtained by in vitro studies using human brain tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we were able to quantify specific benzodiazepines in vivo in the brain.
the Bmax values of the central-type benzodiazpines in human brain were similar to those in animal brain.

PET with [11C]Ro 15-1789 can be used to measure the Bmax and K(d) for central-type benzodiazapine receptors, which may provide a useful tool for the quantitative in vivo characterization of these receptors in humans.
